source_text: Regula exigit ueritatis ut primo omnium credamus in deum patrem et dominum omnipotentem, id est, rerum omnium perfectissimum conditorem, qui caelum alta sublimitate suspenderit, terram deiecta mole solidauerit, maria soluto liquore diffuderit, et haec omnia propriis et condignis instrumentis et ornata et plena digesserit. nam et in solidamento caeli luciferos solis ortus excitauit, lunae candentem globum ad solacium noctis mensurnis incrementis orbis impleuit, astrorum etiam radios uariis fulgoribus micantis lucis accendit: et haec omnia legitimis meatibus circumire totum mundi ambitum uoluit, humano generi dies, menses, annos, signa, tempora, utilitatesque factura. in terris quoque altissimos montes in uerticem sustulit, ualles in ima deiecit, campos aequaliter strauit, animalium greges ad uarias hominum seruitutes utiliter instituit. siluarum quoque robora humanis usibus profutura solidauit, fruges in cibum elicuit, fontium ora reserauit, et lapsuris fluminibus infudit. post quae, ne non etiam ipsis quoque deliciis procurasset oculorum, uariis florum coloribus ad uoluptatem spectantium cuncta uestiuit. in ipso quoque mari, quamuis esset et magnitudine et utilitate mirabile, multimoda animalia, nunc mediocris, nunc uasticorporis fingit, ingenium artificis de institutionis uarietate testantia. quibus non contentus, ne forte fremitus et cursus aquarum, cum dispendio possessoris humani, alienum occuparet elementum, fines litoribus inclusit: quo cum fremens fluctus et ex alto sinu spumans unda uenisset, rursum in se rediret nec terminos concessos excederet, seruans iura praescripta: ut diuinas leges tanto magis homo custodiret, quanto illas etiam elementa seruassent. Post quae hominem quoque mundo praeposuit et quidem ad imaginem dei factum: cui mentem et rationem indidit et prudentiam, ut deum posset imitari: cuius etsi corporis terrena primordia, caelestis tamen et diuini halitus inspirata substantia: quem, cum omnia in seruitutem illi dedisset, solum liberum esse uoluit. et ne in periculum caderet rursum soluta libertas, mandatum posuit, quo tamen non inesse malum fructu arboris doceretur, sed futurum, si forte, ex uoluntate hominis de contemptu datae legis praemonenam et liber esse debuerat, ne incongruenter dei imago seruiret: et lex addenda, ne usque ad contemptum dantis libertas effrenata prorumperet: ut et praemia condigna et merita poenarum consequenter exciperet, suum iam habens illud, quod motu mentis in alterutram partem agitare uoluisset. ex quo mortalitas, inuidia utique, in ipsum redit; qui cum illam de oboedientia posset euadere, in eandem incurrit, dum ex consilio peruerso deus esse festinat. cuius tamen poenam nihilominus indulgenter temperauit, dum non tam ipse, quam labores eius maledicuntur super terra. nam et quod requiritur, non ex ignorantia uenit, sed spem hominis futurae in Christo et inuentionis et salutis ostendit: et quod ne de ligno arboris uitae contingat arcetur, non de inuidiae maligno liuore descendit, sed ne uiuens in aeternum, nisi peccata Christus ante donasset, circumferret secum in poenam sui semper immortale delictum. Quamquam etiam superioribus, id est, super ipsum quoque solidamentum partibus, quae non sunt hodie nostris contemplabiles oculis, angelos prius instituerit, spiritales uirtutes digesserit, thronos potestatesque praefecerit, et alia multa caelorum immensa spatia et sacramentorum infinita opera condiderit, ut immensus hic licet mundus paene nouissimum magis dei corporalium rerum appareat opus esse, quam solum, namque quae infra terram iacent, neque ipsa sunt digestis et ordinatis potestatibus uacua. locus enim est quo piorum animae impiorumque ducuntur, futuri iudicii praeiudicia sentientes: ut operum ipsius in omnibus partibus redundantes magnitudines non intra mundi huius capacissimos licet, ut diximus, sinus conclusas uideremus, sed etiam infra ipsius mundi et profunda et altitudines cogitare possemus; et sic considerata operum magnitudine, tantae molis digne mirari possemus artificem.
pass_a_gloss: The rule of truth demands that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord, all-powerful, that is, the most perfect creator of all things, who has suspended the heaven with high sublimity, solidified the earth with a thrown-down mass, poured out the seas with a loosened liquid, and has arranged and filled all these things with their own and worthy instruments. For also in the solidification of the heaven, He has excited the light-bringing sunrises, filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of the orbit for the solace of night, and ignited the rays of the stars with various gleams of twinkling light. And He has willed that all these things go around the whole circuit of the world with legitimate paths, making days, months, years, signs, times, and utilities for the human race. On the earth, He has also lifted up the highest mountains to a peak, thrown down the valleys to the lowest point, and evenly laid out the fields, and has usefully instituted the herds of animals for various human services. He has also solidified the strength of the forests for human uses, brought forth the crops for food, opened the mouths of the springs, and poured into the flowing rivers. After these things, so that He might also have provided for the delights of the eyes, He has clothed all things with various flower colors for the pleasure of the onlookers. In the sea itself, although it was wonderful in magnitude and utility, He has fashioned many kinds of animals, now of moderate size, now of vast body, testifying to the ingenuity of the artisan from the variety of institutions. Not content with these things, lest perhaps the roar and course of the waters, with the loss of the human possessor, might occupy an alien element, He has enclosed the shores with boundaries, so that when the foaming wave and the spuming surge came, it would return into itself and not exceed the granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws, so that man might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements kept them. After these things, He has also placed man in the world, and indeed made in the image of God, to whom He has given a mind and reason and prudence, so that he might imitate God. Although the earthly beginnings of his body, the substance of his breath is inspired by the heavenly and divine, and He has willed that he be the only free one, after having given all things into his service. And lest he fall into danger, with his freedom loosened, He has given a command, by which, however, the evil of the fruit of the tree is not taught to be present, but future, if perhaps, from the will of man, from contempt of the given law, He has forewarned, and he ought to be free, lest the image of God serve incongruously. And the law is added, lest the unbridled freedom burst forth up to the contempt of the giver, so that he might receive the worthy rewards and the deserved punishments, having that which he had willed to agitate with the motion of his mind to one side or the other. From this, mortality, certainly envy, returns to him, who, since he could have escaped from obedience, falls into the same, while hastening to be God from perverted counsel. Nevertheless, God has tempered his punishment indulgently, while not he himself, but his labors are cursed above the earth. For what is required does not come from ignorance, but shows the hope of man for the future in Christ and the invention and salvation, and what is forbidden lest one touch the tree of life does not come from the malignant envy, but lest, living eternally, he might carry with him into punishment his always immortal delict, unless Christ had previously given sins. Although even in the things above, that is, above the solidification itself, which are not visible to our eyes today, He has previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual virtues, and appointed thrones and powers, and has founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of sacraments, so that this immense world might seem to be almost the last, rather than the only, work of God's bodily things, for the things that lie beneath the earth are not empty of arranged and ordered powers. For there is a place where the souls of the pious and the impious are led, experiencing the pre-judgments of the future judgment, so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of His works only within the most capacious bosom of this world, but also consider them beneath the depths and heights of the world itself, and thus, considering the magnitude of the works, we might be able to wonder worthily at the artisan of such great works.

pass_b_english: The rule of truth requires us first of all to believe in God the Father and Lord, the Almighty — the most perfect Creator of all things. He suspended the heavens with high sublimity, solidified the earth with a thrown-down mass, poured out the seas with loosened liquid, and arranged and filled all these things with their own proper and worthy instruments. In the firmament He stirred up the light‑bringing sunrises, filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of its orbit for the solace of night, and kindled the rays of the stars with various gleams of twinkling light. He willed that all these bodies traverse the whole circuit of the world along legitimate paths, producing days, months, years, signs, seasons, and benefits for the human race. On the earth He lifted the highest mountains to their peaks, sank the valleys to their lowest depths, spread the plains evenly, and usefully established herds of animals for the varied services of humanity. He also strengthened the timber of the forests for human use, brought forth crops for food, opened the mouths of springs, and fed the flowing rivers. After these things, so that He might also provide for the delight of the eyes, He clothed everything with the varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of those who look on them. In the sea itself, though it was already wonderful in magnitude and utility, He fashioned many kinds of creatures, now of moderate size, now of vast bulk, testifying to the artisan's ingenuity through the variety of their forms. Not content with these, lest the roar and surge of the waters, to the loss of the human possessor, should invade an alien element, He enclosed the shores with boundaries, so that when the foaming wave and the spuming surge came they would turn back into themselves and not exceed the granted limits, keeping the prescribed laws, that man might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements observed them. After these things He also placed man in the world, made in the image of God. He gave him mind, reason, and prudence so that he might imitate God. Although his body had earthly origins, the substance of his breath was inspired by the heavenly and divine. And after giving all things into his service, He willed that man alone should be free. And lest he fall into danger with his freedom unloosed, He gave a command — not to teach that evil was present in the fruit of the tree, but that it would be future, if perhaps, from man's will, from contempt of the given law; He forewarned him, and man ought to be free, lest the image of God serve incongruously. And the law was added lest unbridled freedom burst forth into contempt of the Giver, so that man might receive worthy rewards and deserved punishments, having the power to agitate his mind's motion toward one side or the other. From this, mortality — certainly envy — returns to him, who, though he could have escaped through obedience, falls into the same condition while hastening to be God from perverse counsel. Nevertheless God tempered his punishment indulgently, cursing not so much the man himself as his labors upon the earth. For what is required does not come from ignorance, but shows the hope of man for the future in Christ, both of discovery and salvation. And the prohibition against touching the tree of life does not spring from malignant envy, but lest, living eternally, man might carry with him into punishment his ever‑immortal offense, unless Christ had previously forgiven sins. Although even in the regions above — above the firmament itself — which are not visible to our eyes today, He previously instituted angels, arranged spiritual virtues, appointed thrones and powers, and founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of mysteries, so that this immense world might appear to be almost the last, rather than the only, work of God's bodily creation. For the things that lie beneath the earth are not empty of ordered and arranged powers. There is a place where the souls of the pious and the impious are led, experiencing the pre‑judgments of the future judgment, so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of His works only within the most capacious bosom of this world, but also consider them beneath the depths and heights of the world itself. And thus, contemplating the magnitude of the works, we may worthily wonder at the Artisan of such great works.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological and cosmological arguments of the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the nuances of the 'tree of life' section and the distinction between the presence and future occurrence of evil. The translation of 'sacramentorum' as 'sacraments' (A) and 'mysteries' (B) is acceptable within patristic contexts. All clauses, including the conditional and causal relations regarding man's freedom and the role of Christ, are preserved.
